claim: The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were created at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference, with voting power weighted by each member's financial quota rather than by population — concentrating control in the wealthiest shareholders led by the United States. By an informal convention that has held unbroken since the institutions opened, the World Bank president has always been a U.S. national nominated by Washington, the Bank's largest shareholder, and the IMF managing director has always been a European.

sources.label: Wikipedia — President of the World Bank Group (the U.S./European nomination convention).
sources.quote: Traditionally, the World Bank Group president has always been an American citizen nominated by the United States, the Bank's largest shareholder, and the IMF's managing director has been a European citizen.

sources.label: Congressional Research Service — “Selecting the World Bank President” (R42463), on the U.S.-nominee tradition.

notes: From @ojas_speaks reel DY0Oj5EpTHZ. The reel says “the president of the World Bank has always been American” (whisper transcribed it as “Royal Bank”) and points to quota-weighted voting; both are accurate. The specific “a British person's vote is worth 41 times” figure in the reel is a quota-weighting illustration that is hard to pin to a single primary, so it is not asserted here — the unbroken U.S.-president convention is the verifiable core.
